transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-03
Time: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Merchant (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Horizon CTO), Sara Nguyen (Eng Lead), Mohamed El-Sayed (Infra), Tina Lee (PM)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be noisy):
Customer evaluating migrating inference away from OpenAI / Anthropic hosted APIs toward either Redwood hosted/dedicated or a private deployment. Primary drivers: cost, latency variability during spikes, and data residency for EU workloads. They currently run a mix of Anthropic and OpenAI for chat + a few self-hosted vLLM instances for internal batch transforms. Key concerns: eval parity (same outputs), throughput on long-context convs, KV cache compatibility, and SSO/KMS integration.

Topics:
- Current stack and pain points
- Migration constraints (timeline, stakeholders, compliance)
- Technical parity (vLLM/TGI differences, tokenization, model variants)
- Deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC)
- Next steps and benchmarks

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Merchant: Hey everyone, thanks for doing this — I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on the account. Quick check, audio ok?
[00:06] Daniel Park: Yeah, sounds good. Thanks for slotting us in, Alex.
[00:09] Alex Merchant: Cool. Priya, do you want to intro on the SE side?
[00:12] Priya Shah: Yep hi all, Priya Shah, I'm the solutions engineer, I'll be the technical lead. We'll try and focus on migration feasibility, parity risks and what a pilot would look like.
[00:22] Sara Nguyen: Great. On our side I'm Sara, leading engineering for the inference platform, and Mohamed runs infra, and Tina is PM for this initiative.
[00:29] Mohamed El-Sayed: Morning.

[00:31] Alex Merchant: Awesome. Daniel, could you give us the short version of what you guys run today and what triggered this exploration?
[00:38] Daniel Park: Sure. We're Horizon DataWorks, we provide analytics + ingestion for financial data. We use OpenAI for customer-facing chat, Anthropic for some safety-sensitive flows, and we also started self-hosting an instance of vLLM for cheaper batch embedding jobs. The main push is costs — token spend increasing 3x YOY — and latency variability from public APIs during peak market hours. Also legal wants control for EU data residency.
[01:05] Alex Merchant: That makes sense. When you say self-hosting vLLM, is that the HuggingFace TGI stack or a different setup?
[01:12] Sara Nguyen: We're running vLLM on Kubernetes, modified TGI forks for faster sampling. It's a bit of a Frankenstein, honestly. We get lower unit cost for batch but it's brittle for low-latency interactive traffic.
[01:23] Priya Shah: Got it. So mixed environment, some hosted, some self-hosted. Do you have a timeline you're aiming for? Migration windows?
[01:31] Tina Lee: We're targeting a pilot by Q1 quarter — so Jan/Feb — with a production roll in H1 if benchmarks match. Legal needs to sign off so some slack there.

[01:40] Mohamed El-Sayed: Also, infra note — our teams can't tolerate too much re-architecture. Anything that requires deep tokenizer or prompt rewriting is a non-starter unless the wins are huge.
[01:51] Alex Merchant: Understood. On parity — customers tend to worry about exact tokenization and generation divergence when moving models/providers. Priya, want to talk about how Redwood addresses eval parity?
[02:00] Priya Shah: Yeah. Short version: we provide model mapping and a compatibility layer for curated open models, and we run eval harnesses with your prompt set to measure regression on key metrics like ROUGE/Exact match and safety heuristics. For customers running vLLM/TGI we validate sampling parameters, temperature, top-p, logits processors and KV cache behavior.
[02:23] Daniel Park: How often do you see drift between OpenAI outputs and an open checkpoint? Our firm cares about reply consistency for audit logs.
[02:32] Priya Shah: It depends. If you're moving off a closed provider to an open checkpoint there's often semantic differences — but we can tune decoding and sometimes recommend a small fine-tune or alignment pass. For the majority of customer prompts we can reach parity within acceptable bounds — and we surface those deltas in a dashboard.
[02:47] Sara Nguyen: You mentioned KV cache behavior — our long-convo workload is very sensitive. We do a lot of incremental chat with 16k+ contexts and rely on cache hits to keep latency low. Does Redwood's runtime expose cache controls?
[03:02] Priya Shah: Yes. The runtime has explicit KV management and prefix caching, with options to persist or evict based on session policies. You can pin certain tokens and we also support sharded KV across GPUs for long contexts. There's some nuance migrating from vLLM because their cache semantics might differ, but it's doable.
[03:20] Mohamed El-Sayed: Ok. Also security/regulatory — we need SSO/SAML, audit logs, customer-managed KMS, and EU data residency for a portion of traffic. Does Redwood Private support that?
[03:33] Alex Merchant: Yes — Redwood Private offers a VPC deploy and on-prem packages, KMS integrations, audit logs and SAML/SSO support. We'll send the security pack after the call.
[03:41] Daniel Park: Does that mean you manage the control plane? We prefer customer-managed control plane for some regs.
[03:46] Priya Shah: We have two models: hosted control plane (Redwood-managed) and a private control plane option where the customer owns the control plane and we provide the runtime and orchestration. Both integrate with KMS and SAML.

[03:58] Alex Merchant: Let's dig into costs briefly — Mohamed, what's your current per-1M token cost from OpenAI and from your self-hosted vLLM infra?
[04:07] Mohamed El-Sayed: Roughly, OpenAI chat around $40-45 / 1M tokens at current consumption levels, Anthropic similar for the longer flows. Our vLLM runs drop it to about $8-10 / 1M when fully utilized but that's for batch, not interactive. The problem is we often can't commit to that utilization for latency traffic.
[04:26] Priya Shah: That's exactly the trade-off Redwood Dedicated tries to solve — predictable capacity (reserved) to hit closer to self-hosted economics for interactive traffic while keeping SLA and support.
[04:36] Tina Lee: For us, a big factor is vendor lock risk — we don't want model outputs changing because the provider changes internal tuning.
[04:43] Alex Merchant: Right. We run pinned model versions and provide immutability windows for rollouts so you can freeze a version for a regulated release.

[04:50] Daniel Park: On the technical side, we have two particular worries: tokenizer divergence and helper tokens used in Anthropic prompts that don't map 1:1 to open models. Any experience there?
[05:02] Priya Shah: Yes — we've seen that with Anthropic system messages and special tokens. We usually map or rewrite system prompts and then measure delta. Sometimes a short fine-tune or few-shot prompt engineering fixes it. We log these changes so you maintain an audit trail.

[05:18] Alex Merchant: Let's talk bench plan — what's the minimal set to evaluate parity and SLA? Priya?
[05:23] Priya Shah: Minimal: 1) a representative prompt set (100-500 prompts spanning convo lengths), 2) latency SLOs (P50/P95 targets), 3) cost snapshot (tokens per month), 4) safety/QA criteria. We'll run the same prompts against your vLLM, Redwood hosted, and a candidate open checkpoint through Redwood's runtime. For long context we'll do cache warmup scenarios.
[05:44] Sara Nguyen: For the prompt set — we'll include a lot of long-chain LLM interactions and regulatory phrasing so we can catch failures.
[05:51] Daniel Park: Timeline for running that?
[05:53] Priya Shah: If you can share prompts this week, we can run initial parity tests within 7-10 days. Full bench (with ops and private deploy validation) within 3 weeks.

[06:03] Mohamed El-Sayed: About the private deploy: do you support air-gapped on-prem? We have a couple of customers in the EU that require it.
[06:10] Priya Shah: Yes, we have an on-prem package; it's more involved and has lead time for licensing, but we do support air-gapped with customer-managed KMS. We'll put the deployment checklist in the security pack.

[06:20] Tina Lee: Any gotchas with TGI forks? We use a modified TGI for performance; worried Redwood won't run our variant out of the box.
[06:28] Priya Shah: We usually have to validate custom kernels and tuning; sometimes that's straightforward, sometimes it requires small changes. We can run a compatibility test on your TGI images in our dedicated lab as part of the pilot.

[06:40] Alex Merchant: Any compliance red flags you want to call out?
[06:42] Daniel Park: Mostly auditability and ability to show model versioning for regulatory exams. Also we need SLA for data purge and legal hold capabilities.
[06:50] Priya Shah: Redwood's audit logs include per-request metadata and model version; we can surface retention and purge endpoints for legal hold. We'll include examples in the docs.

[07:00] (brief pause / side chatter)
[07:10] Sara Nguyen: Practical question — if we do hosted Redwood API for a subset of traffic and Dedicated for others, is routing supported between tiers? For example, risk-sensitive flows to dedicated or private, general chat to hosted.
[07:23] Priya Shah: Yes, you can route by policy: model, route, customer segment, or latency. We have fallback policies too — if dedicated is saturated it can fall back to hosted with a different model.
[07:34] Mohamed El-Sayed: How does billing look if we route between tiers? We need a clear cost breakdown per token per route.
[07:41] Alex Merchant: The console offers token-level cost breakdown and per-route dashboards. Pricing sheet will detail hosted per-token vs dedicated reserved capacity amortized cost.

[07:50] Daniel Park: Ok let's get more granular on parity: do you have examples of customers who moved from OpenAI to curated open checkpoints and what their delta looked like?
[07:59] Priya Shah: Yes, we had a finance customer who moved from a closed provider to a 70B open checkpoint; they saw small changes in tone and a 3-5% drop in certain extraction metrics but we recovered most via prompt tuning and a small supervised reweighting step. We can share anonymized case notes.
[08:17] Tina Lee: Are there automated regression alerts? We want to know if a rollout changes key metrics.
[08:22] Priya Shah: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitors and regression alerts tied to your eval sets, with threshold-based alerts.

[08:30] Alex Merchant: Any blockers on your side for starting the pilot?
[08:33] Daniel Park: We need legal to look at the private deployment contract and we need to confirm sample data sharing for benchmarks. Also want to make sure the bench won't require us to rework tokenization.
[08:44] Priya Shah: We'll keep tokenization agnostic where possible and document any changes. For the contract, Alex will follow up with a starter.

[08:52] (noise, unclear)
[08:55] Mohamed El-Sayed: One more infra note: we'd like to measure tail latency at P99 for long contexts — can Redwood expose those metrics in real time?
[09:03] Priya Shah: Yes — per-route latency, P50/P95/P99 and token throughput. We can also stream traces to your observability stack (e.g., Datadog).

[09:12] Alex Merchant: Great. I'll summarize next steps — Alex to send pricing and contract starter; Priya to own bench plan and test harness; Daniel to share prompt set and cost numbers; schedule technical deep-dive. Any objections?
[09:26] Daniel Park: Sounds good. One ask — can the benchmark run use our modified TGI binary? It's critical to prove parity on our actual stack.
[09:33] Priya Shah: Yes, we can accept your binary or run it in your account if easier. We'll include details in the bench plan.

[09:40] Tina Lee: Also interested in a high-level migration playbook — step-by-step for devs and legal.
[09:45] Alex Merchant: We'll include a migration playbook and runbook with rollback steps and QA gates.

[09:50] (wrap up)
[09:52] Alex Merchant: Ok thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the security pack, pricing sheet, and bench plan. Expect emails from us in the next 48 hours.
[09:59] Daniel Park: Thanks, appreciate it.

End of transcript.
